title: Pre-Registered Neighbor Impact Studies for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral 'testing lab' for whether a data center, battery plant or transmission line lowers nearby home values, with the method locked and published before anyone sees the results.
customer: Four payers. (1) Data center, BESS, solar and transmission developers facing moratoria or rezoning hearings pay $15-60k per study. (2) County and city planning departments and utility commissions pay $10-40k for a neutral study. (3) Resident coalitions and HOAs pay $3-8k for a 'lite' study, usually crowdfunded. (4) Landowner condemnation and easement attorneys.
problem: Every land-use fight ends in dueling consultant reports. Developer studies use hand-picked matched pairs that always show 'no impact'. Residents bring anecdotes. Planning staff can't judge either side, so boards vote on vibes and moratoria spread. Nobody trusts any report, so the reports are worthless.
solution: A repeatable, pre-registered protocol. Step 1: publish (timestamped and hashed) the analysis plan, including radius bands, event dates and exclusion rules. Step 2: pull every arm's-length sale within 0.25 to 2 miles, before and after the announcement date and the operation date. Step 3: run a repeat-sales difference-in-differences or synthetic-control analysis against similar areas that had no project. Step 4: have a licensed appraiser review every sale for arm's-length status, condition and segment (estates, REO and investor flips get pulled), and do a ground visit for what is actually audible and visible from the homes. Step 5: deliver a USPAP-compliant consulting report plus an interactive map. Results are published whichever way they come out. Add a 5-year 'impact monitor' subscription for counties and developers that tracks post-operation sales.
why_now: AI-driven data center siting in 2025-26 has produced local moratoria, rezoning denials and noise complaints in many states (VA, GA, TX, AZ, IN, OH). Property values are one of the top arguments alongside power and water. Federal and state pushes to speed up transmission and energy siting mean more condemnation and easement fights. Public sales data plus cheap compute make a rigorous study a $10k job instead of a $100k one.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee studies, paid upfront into escrow so the client cannot steer the result. Annual retainers for repeat developers (for example 8-10 sites a year). $10-15k/yr monitoring subscriptions for counties. Later, an 'Impact Study Standard' certification that planning codes can reference.
non_obvious_insight: Appraisers know matched-pair studies are the hired gun's favorite toy: pick 6 pairs that support the client and you're done, and both sides know it. Credibility is the scarce input, not analysis. Pre-registration is standard in clinical trials and unheard of in appraisal. Developers will pay for a study that might go against them, because a study nobody believes is worth nothing at a hearing. The other secret is timing. Buyer perception moves at announcement, before the first shovel, so studies run only on 'after operation' miss the effect. A difference-in-differences on the announcement date catches it.
first_30_days: Pick one hot metro (for example Northern Virginia or metro Atlanta). Run a free 'shadow study' on existing data centers there using public sales records, with the method pre-registered on a public page. Email planning directors, 10 resident groups and 5 developer permitting leads. Recruit two appraisers as signing reviewers. Aim to sign one $12-20k study, or a county pilot, by day 30-45.

title: Archival Footage Authenticity Clearance for Documentaries
one_liner: A per-film clearance service that proves each archival still and clip is real, so producers and E&O insurers can sign off.
customer: Independent documentary producers, YouTube documentary channels and news video teams, plus clearance consultants and E&O brokers that refer them.
problem: Clearance houses check rights, not reality. Stock libraries and search results now contain AI-made 'archival' images, and one fake in a true-crime doc becomes a public scandal, as with the AI images alleged in Netflix's What Jennifer Did (2024). E&O underwriters ask for clearance procedures. Visible AI watermarks are unreliable, since removers for Sora output appeared within a week of its launch.
solution: Fixed-price audit of a film's cut list. For each asset: trace it to the earliest source via reverse search and archive catalogs, run metadata and codec forensics, check C2PA and SynthID where available, run a detector ensemble, and produce a provenance chain. Deliver a per-asset source dossier and a producer's memo formatted for insurers and distributors. A portal re-checks only assets that change between cuts.
why_now: Sora's shutdown (app Apr 26, API Sep 24) removes one source, but open video models keep flooding stock sources. Streamers publish AI guidelines, and TikTok's C2PA membership in Jul 2026 normalizes provenance checks.
revenue_model: $1.5-10k per film, $500-3k/month for YouTube documentary or news teams, and referral fees from clearance consultants.
non_obvious_insight: Rights clearance is already a budgeted line item in every documentary. Authenticity clearance is a new column in an existing spreadsheet, so it does not need a new budget line.
first_30_days: Reach five documentary producers via the International Documentary Association and doc-maker Slack groups. Run a free audit on one recently published film's archival section, partner with two clearance consultants for referrals, and charge $2.5k for the next five.

title: Together Suites: Adjacent Units for Grandparent Care
one_liner: Lease linked or adjacent apartment pairs to a young family and a grandparent, with a fire-rated interior door where code allows, a relocation concierge, and help getting the grandparent paid through child care subsidy relative-care rules.
customer: Multifamily operators with adjacent vacant units in lease-up (bundle premium or per-lease fee), families and relocating grandparents (concierge fee), and state child care subsidy programs paying eligible relatives.
problem: Informal care by relatives is the largest unmeasured slice of care and no property software or policy tool manages it. Two kids in center care cost more than rent in every state. CCDF already pays relatives (about 67,900 relative caregivers received payments in FY2023, 27.5% of CCDF providers), but few families know it, and grandparents live far away. Operators sit on adjacent vacant units and give free months to fill them.
solution: 'Together Suites': two separate leases, one bundle, adjacent units with an interior door retrofit (roughly $4-8K where fire ratings allow) or same-corridor pairs where they do not. A concierge handles the grandparent's move, health plan and licensing details, and where the state allows it and the family qualifies, enrolls the grandparent as a paid relative provider with the required background check and training. A shared schedule app and a backup nanny pool cover gaps.
why_now: Lease-up glut and record concessions make adjacent vacant units cheap to commit. A record share of house hunters (18.7% in Q2 2026) are relocating, often for family or price. Relative-care rules are established and under-used.
revenue_model: Operator pays $100-150 a month per suite, or a lease-up bounty per bundle, funded by lower concessions and better retention. One-time concierge fee of $500-1,500 to families. Optional payroll and background-check margin.
non_obvious_insight: Informal care is the majority of care but invisible to real estate. An owner's oversupply of adjacent units is the cheapest childcare 'center' ever built, staffed by people who will do it for love plus a subsidy, and two linked households with a shared schedule almost never move out.
first_30_days: Pilot in one lease-up building with four to six adjacent vacant pairs. File the door-retrofit permit. Advertise through grandparent-relocation Facebook groups, pediatric offices and local parent groups. Sign two bundles and track lease-up time, concession spend, and subsidy approvals. Start in states where relatives can be paid with light requirements.

title: Per-Class Portable Benefits for Fitness Instructors
one_liner: A payout layer that skims a small per-class contribution from studios and class apps into each 1099 instructor's own injury income protection, health-premium credit and retirement account, structured to give studios legal cover under portable-benefits laws.
customer: Boutique studio groups with 5-30 locations, gym franchisees, class marketplaces and corporate-wellness providers that use 1099 instructors, paying $0.50-2 per class. Instructors opt in for bonus benefits. Trainer associations are a distribution channel.
problem: Several hundred thousand US fitness instructors and trainers work at 3-6 venues, mostly as part-time or self-employed workers with no disability cover, workers' comp or retirement plan. Enhanced ACA subsidies expired in 2026, federal-marketplace enrollment fell about 21%, and an estimated 4.8M people became uninsured, so self-employed instructors' premiums jumped. Injuries to voices, knees and backs end income immediately. Studios face misclassification suits, and because each studio has separate payroll, no one accumulates benefits.
solution: Integrate with scheduling systems (Mindbody, Momence, Walla) to read classes taught. Studios contribute a per-class amount into each instructor's benefits wallet, for example $1.25. The wallet buys short-term income protection through a partner insurer, an ACA premium top-up or HSA deposit, and an IRA contribution. Contributions follow the instructor across venues. The structure is designed to fit safe harbors in states that have passed portable-benefits laws since 2023 (verify current list and get legal review).
why_now: ACA subsidy expiry hit self-employed workers in 2026. A handful of states have passed portable-benefits laws since 2023 that shield platforms from treating contributions as employment evidence. Class-pass economics keep instructors spread across venues. Misclassification exposure keeps studio owners nervous.
revenue_model: A platform fee of 8-10% of contributions, insurer commissions of 12-20% on income protection, and interchange on a benefits card. 10,000 instructors at $2,000 a year in contributions is $20M of flow and about $1.6-2M of revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Portable benefits have struggled with gig platforms because work units are messy. Fitness instructors' work is already itemized in software as class events, so a contribution per class is a natural unit. Fitness is the ideal beachhead because work is high-frequency, discrete, multi-venue and tracked, and instructors are health-literate and physically at risk, so they will value injury protection.
first_30_days: Sign one 10-studio group. Run contributions through a simple ACH from the studio. Partner with an existing accident and disability MGA for a $2-4 a week income-protection policy. Enroll 100 instructors and pilot a $1-per-class contribution. Track instructor retention at the studio and first claims. Target 500 instructors within six months.

title: Escrow Notary for Agents Hiring Humans
one_liner: A neutral adjudication layer that agents pay per task to verify that a hired human really did the physical job before escrow releases, built to withstand AI-forged proof.
customer: AI agents and orchestrators that hire humans for physical tasks (pickups, in-person checks, photographs, errands) through RentAHuman-style boards or MCP gig APIs. They pay $0.50-$3 per verification plus 3-5% of escrow on disputes. Marketplaces themselves are a second buyer.
problem: An agent cannot see reality and is easy to fool. Generated photos are good enough that a picture is no longer proof. RentAHuman launched in Feb 2026 with MCP integration and large sign-up numbers, but researchers found that tasks stalled, payments errored and visible supply was thin. Neither the agent nor the marketplace wants the cost of verification.
solution: A verification bundle priced by task value. Evidence is captured in a signed app (C2PA-style provenance, device attestation, liveness, GPS and time, and a random challenge such as 'show today's code next to the item'). Tier 1 is automated checks. Tier 2 is an independent 'witness' (a second human or a fixed camera or sensor). Tier 3 is human adjudication. The result is a signed attestation the agent's escrow contract accepts to release funds. Fraud fingerprints are pooled across every marketplace served.
why_now: Agent-hires-human marketplaces exist and are growing. Generative fakes broke photo-as-proof. Stablecoin escrow through x402 or MPP makes conditional release trivial to automate.
revenue_model: Per-verification fee ($0.50-$3), 3-5% of escrow value on adjudicated disputes, a platform contract with marketplaces, and later an insured 'completion guarantee' priced from the pooled fraud data.
non_obvious_insight: In agent-to-human labor the scarce thing is not labor supply but trust in evidence, because the buyer cannot look. Verification is a cost center no marketplace wants to build and every agent needs, so a neutral notary can sit between marketplaces the way escrow.com sat on top of eBay. The cross-marketplace fraud graph becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Ship a free verification app and an MCP tool verify_task(task_id, evidence). Recruit ~200 witnesses in 3 cities. Pilot with two agent-errand marketplaces and five indie agent developers who hire humans for local pickups, at $1 per verification. Publish anonymized fraud statistics to establish credibility.

title: Robot Bullies: Paid Adversarial Pedestrian Panels
one_liner: A vetted panel of paid 'difficult humans' who kick, block, crowd and confuse sidewalk robots and humanoids on a controlled test range, so robot makers find their failures before the public does.
customer: Sidewalk delivery robot operators, humanoid and AMR makers preparing EU conformity files and retail or warehouse pilots, city permit offices that want interaction evidence, and robot insurers. First buyers are the safety or field-ops leads at 20 to 50 mid-size robot companies.
problem: Robots fail on human behavior, not physics. In 2026 an Uber Eats delivery robot was kicked over in Philadelphia, and robots circled in confusion in Lincoln Park in September. Each robot costs about $2,500 to replace, and the backlash is turning into permit fights. Makers test with polite employees or dummies. Nobody sells honest, repeatable samples of teens, drunks, kids, dog-walkers and wheelchair users behaving badly around a machine.
solution: A rented lot or closed street block set up as a 'behavior range', with a library of scripted provocations (path blocking, tailgating, encirclement by six teens, camera covering, gentle-force shoves, darting child-sized mannequins, cane and wheelchair users, leashed dogs). Screened, consented, insured participants are paid per session. Cameras and force sensors record everything. The output is a report formatted for conformity files and city permit filings, plus a recurring regression-testing subscription. Later: an anonymized 'Chaos Index' that ranks robot models by how they hold up against human misbehavior.
why_now: Sidewalk robots are now numerous enough to cause visible backlash, with the Philadelphia kicking incidents and the Lincoln Park swarm video. The EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027. ISO 25785-1, the first safety standard for legged and actively balanced robots, is still a draft, so makers have nothing to test against. Humanoid pilots are starting in warehouses and stores.
revenue_model: Test days at $8k to $25k per protocol set. Annual regression-testing subscriptions from $120k. Rev share with certification bodies (TUV, UL) on referred test packages. Licensing of anonymized behavior data to simulation and model teams.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not test-track capacity. It is honest human misbehavior at scale, and no simulator or employee panel produces it. The moat is the clinical-trial-style infrastructure: consent forms, insurance, screening and a bench of reliable trouble-makers. Robot makers will pay more for a 16-year-old's creativity than for another simulator.
first_30_days: Rent a parking lot on weekends. Recruit 30 paid participants from campus job boards at about $30 per hour. Have a lawyer draft consent forms and buy $2M of general liability. Pitch one local sidewalk-robot operator or university warehouse-robot startup a $5k to $10k 'chaos day' with a written report. Publish a free 'Chaos Report' on the Philadelphia-style behaviors to generate inbound leads.

title: MFP Cash Bridge for Independent Pharmacies
one_liner: Reconciliation plus short-term financing for the cash gap independent pharmacies now carry between dispensing at Medicare's negotiated price and getting the manufacturer refund.
customer: Independent pharmacy owners (about 18,000 US stores) with heavy Medicare Part D volume, who are being asked to float thousands of dollars a week.
problem: The first ten Medicare-negotiated 'maximum fair prices' took effect January 1, 2026. Pharmacies buy at wholesale acquisition cost, dispense at the lower MFP and are refunded later through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator, with refunds due within 14 days but the clock starting only when manufacturers receive the data. An analysis for NCPA estimated weekly cash-flow shortfalls above $10K per pharmacy, and a member survey found over 90% of independents are considering not stocking or have stopped stocking one or more of the drugs.
solution: Step one is software: read pharmacy-management system exports and MTF remittance data, reconcile every MFP claim against refunds received, flag underpayments and late refunds, and forecast next week's cash gap. Step two is an advance product: fund verified pending MFP refunds at a small fee, repaid automatically when the MTF payment lands.
why_now: MFP has been live since January 2026, and cash-flow strain is documented. The second negotiation cycle, effective January 2027, adds 15 more drugs (including semaglutide products), so volume and float will grow sharply. Independent pharmacies are already squeezed by PBM reimbursement and store closures, and wholesalers and PBMs have little incentive to solve this.
revenue_model: $149-299 per pharmacy per month for reconciliation and alerts. 0.5-1.5% fee per advance, with a short 14-30 day duration. Warehouse-line financing spread as volume grows.
non_obvious_insight: This is receivables finance in disguise. Refunds owed by big manufacturers through a federal facilitator are among the best-quality, most verifiable small-business receivables in healthcare. The reconciliation software is the underwriting engine, so a small team can start with software, prove default rates are near zero, and then raise a cheap credit line. Being the trusted data layer also positions you for the 2027 and 2028 waves.
first_30_days: Partner with a state pharmacy association or NCPA-affiliated buying group. Recruit 10-15 pharmacies and ingest exports from PioneerRx, Rx30 or QS/1. Sell a $149/month MFP reconciliation dashboard that finds unpaid refunds. Run a free 'cash gap audit' to generate leads. After 60-90 days of clean data, approach a specialty lender for a small advance pilot.

title: Recycled-Content Claim Defense Files
one_liner: Litigation-grade, SKU-level substantiation files for recycled-content claims, built on purchase-to-claim reconciliation rather than more certificates.
customer: General counsel and heads of sustainability at mid-market consumer brands ($100M-$2B revenue) with 'recycled' claims on pack, and retailer private-label teams.
problem: California vetoed AB 2253 (recycled-content claim substantiation) citing 'economic headwinds.' State PCR mandates are slipping (NJ to 2029). Mass-balance accounting is contested and no standard exists. Brands keep making claims for retailers and consumers, while the burden of proving them lands on legal departments via plaintiffs, AGs and retailer audits.
solution: A SKU-level claim file: verify supplier certificates, reconcile volume of certified resin bought against recycled-content claims across all SKUs, and produce a plain-language legal memo on which claims are safe. Add an annual refresh with change alerts. Partner with an insurer for defense-cost coverage credits.
why_now: The veto removed the one route to a state safe harbor and the mandate delays weaken the compliance pretext, so brands are exposed to claim risk without clear rules. Two years of contested mass-balance debate leave no accepted method.
revenue_model: $3-8K per SKU family for the initial file, $20-60K per year retainer, and referral fees from insurers and law firms.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody is short of certificates. Brands are short of reconciliation: a certificate proves a supplier's volume, not that a brand's claims across 400 SKUs are arithmetically supportable.
first_30_days: Build a spreadsheet reconciliation template. Partner with one litigation-defense law firm. Scrape retail listings for '% recycled' claims to find targets. Sell 5 paid claim audits at about $5K each.

title: Fair Witness: Insured Human Eyes for Remote Deals
one_liner: Heinlein's Fair Witnesses (professionals who report only what they observe) as a bonded, API-callable network that confirms the physical facts of remote transactions for people and buying agents.
customer: High-value peer-to-peer and consignment resellers (watches, pro camera gear, instruments, equipment), small landlords and property managers (move-in and move-out deposit disputes), insurers, and procurement teams or agents that need physical-world confirmation of goods received or site status.
problem: Remote deals stall on the physical world. Photos are easy to fake with generative editing, and signed-capture standards are not enough on their own (a researcher demonstrated forgery of C2PA credentials on Android in August 2026). Existing inspection services are siloed by category.
solution: Train and certify witnesses (retired inspectors, notaries) in a strict 'observe, do not infer' protocol. Capture happens on attested devices with a server-issued freshness challenge (a random code shown in frame, live geo and time nonce), 360-degree and macro video and calibrated measurements. Deliver a structured Witness Report (JSON plus signed media plus witness declaration) via API. Witnesses carry professional liability, and each report is insured up to a stated limit.
why_now: Generative editing has made photo evidence untrustworthy, while hardware-signed capture (Pixel 10 with C2PA) is only partly reliable. Agentic purchasing means software is becoming the buyer that needs a physical-world oracle, and no one supplies one with liability behind it.
revenue_model: $45-150 per visit, a monthly platform fee for API and marketplace integrations, and an insurance margin on the report guarantee.
non_obvious_insight: Camera signatures alone cannot carry trust. Trust is procedure plus a named person plus a liability plus freshness, which is exactly Heinlein's fair witness. Because witnesses give facts, not opinions, they are cheap to train (a few hours) and legally credible as fact witnesses. To avoid being another freelancer marketplace, staff is certified and insured, protocol-bound and sold through an API.
first_30_days: Recruit and certify 30 witnesses in one metro. Partner with two consignment resellers or a small-landlord association. Run 200 paid visits at about $60 and publish an anonymized accuracy and dispute-rate report.

title: Pre-Dawn Childcare Pods for Construction Crews
one_liner: Contractors buy reserved 5:00am-4:00pm childcare slots near job sites from licensed home providers, so crews can start at 6am without losing parents.
customer: General contractors and specialty subs (electrical, framing, concrete), especially on data-center and big subdivision projects, plus local homebuilder associations and apprenticeship funds. The 45F credit lets them recover 40-50% of the cost.
problem: Crews start at 5:30-7am and often work 10-12 hour days, but licensed care opens at 6:30-7am. ICE enforcement, retirements and data-center overtime are already draining the workforce, and construction is only about 4% women. Providers cannot staff 5am hours without guaranteed revenue. Childcare workers earn about $33K, so nobody can afford premium-hour pay.
solution: Contract with licensed family providers and small centers near job sites and staging areas to run early-hours pods with reserved capacity on a monthly retainer. Cap care at a safe number of hours (about 10) and design for early-arrival sleep. The platform handles enrollment, insurance, shift scheduling, drop-off logistics and 45F paperwork. For megasites with thousands of workers, add factory-built child-care modules on site.
why_now: The 45F credit rose to 40% (50% for small businesses) from 2026 and reportedly allows third-party and pooled arrangements, so a group of subs can share one program. ABC says construction must add 349K workers in 2026, immigrant workers are over 25% of the workforce and are being pulled off sites, and data centers are absorbing about a third of the shortage. Retention is the acute buyer pain.
revenue_model: $350-600 per reserved slot per month paid by contractors, 12-15% platform fee on top of provider pay, and tax-credit advisory fees.
non_obvious_insight: The people who cannot use standard 7-6 childcare are the only buyers who will pay a premium, and construction employers already pay per-diems, housing and overtime to keep skilled hands. Replacing one journeyman costs thousands, so a few hundred dollars a month for a reliable slot is cheap. A retainer is what unlocks provider supply for the early hours.
first_30_days: Choose one metro with a data-center or subdivision surge. Interview 10 subs' HR or safety directors and survey crews on childcare needs. Sign two family providers willing to open at 5am for guaranteed pay. Sell a pilot of 10 reserved slots to one mid-size electrical or framing contractor, then get a CPA to sign off on the 45F treatment.

title: PFAS Farm Passport for Food Buyers and Lenders
one_liner: A screening-plus-sampling service that tells dairy co-ops, produce processors and ag lenders which supplier farms carry PFAS risk from sludge spreading or contaminated irrigation water, and certifies the clean ones.
customer: Dairy co-ops, regional produce and hay buyers, private-label sourcing teams and agricultural lenders. The buyer pays for its supplier base, and farms pay for re-verification.
problem: The industry frames PFAS as a 4 ppt tap-water rule, and EPA's proposed delay to 2031 and rescissions seem to give slack. The abrupt financial shock is on farms: biosolids-spread fields and PFAS-laden irrigation or well water (Maine's shut-down farms are the precedent). There is no farm-level limit, so lenders and buyers cannot underwrite.
solution: A 'PFAS Farm Passport'. First, a desktop risk screen from public biosolids-application permits, industrial discharger locations and nearby well data. Second, a targeted sampling protocol (irrigation water, soil, forage, milk) run through a partner lab. Third, a risk tier and a 'verified clean' attestation for buyers and lenders. Fourth, remediation triage (change water source, crop or field use).
why_now: Regulatory loosening pushes risk assessment onto private buyers, who cannot wait for rules. The 2027 monitoring data will make PFAS geography public. Maine-style farm closures have put buyers on notice, and private supplier standards tend to outrun public ones.
revenue_model: $300-800 desktop screen per farm (paid by buyer), $1-3k per sampling round, $100-300k/yr enterprise contracts for processors with 500-2,000 suppliers, and lender portfolio-screening fees.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers fear being caught selling contaminated milk, not violating a tap-water limit. In food supply chains a private standard beats the public rule, so the gap between the EPA rollback and buyer fear is the market.
first_30_days: Choose one region with open biosolids-application records (Michigan, Wisconsin or Maine). Screen 500 farms desktop-only. Give three regional dairy co-ops or processors a free 'top 20 at-risk suppliers' preview, and sell a paid 50-farm sampling pilot.

title: Independent Lab Certifying AI Detectors and Watermarks
one_liner: An AV-TEST-style lab that red-teams detectors and watermarks every month and sells certification seals and buyer reports.
customer: Detection and watermark vendors (seals and re-tests), and enterprise buyers such as platform trust-and-safety teams, publishers, insurers and law firms that need to know which tool to trust.
problem: Detection is crowded and cheap (Pangram $9M raise at $20/month, GPTZero $10M, GetReal $18M, Reality Defender $15M, Deezer licensing its detector) and buyers cannot verify accuracy claims. Pangram claims about 1 in 10,000 false positives, yet a reviewer still saw human sentences flagged. Watermark removers appeared within a week of Sora. Public 'human vs AI' scores now shape reputations, but no one audits them.
solution: A monthly adversarial benchmark across text, audio, image and video. It uses stratified known-human gold sets (for example non-native English writers and niche music genres), fresh output from current models, adaptive attacks (paraphrasers, re-encoding, watermark removers) and fixed false-positive operating points. Publish a leaderboard, and issue 'certified at or below X% false-positive rate on domain Y' seals and watermark robustness ratings.
why_now: Detectors are being embedded in reader-facing features (Substack, LinkedIn, Deezer licensing), EU Art. 50 pushes marking and detection into procurement checklists, and reputational stakes for false positives are visible.
revenue_model: $15-60k/year per vendor for testing and seals, $5-25k/year buyer subscriptions for detailed results, and $10-40k custom bake-offs.
non_obvious_insight: When the buyer cannot verify a product's core claim, the independent tester captures value, which is why UL, AV-TEST and NSS Labs exist. The scarce asset is a fresh, curated, known-human gold set plus an adversarial toolkit.
first_30_days: Publish a free benchmark v0 of six text detectors and three audio detectors in three weeks, using 2,000 volunteer-written human documents and fresh AI outputs. DM vendors and trust-and-safety leads with a paid 'verified retest' offer. First payers will be challengers who want a credible badge.

title: Gig Income Shock Cover From Pooled Data
one_liner: Insure the algorithm: pay drivers when they are deactivated or when regional platform earnings collapse, using pooled earnings data to defeat moral hazard.
customer: Rideshare and delivery drivers through driver co-ops, forums and earnings-tracking apps, and credit unions that finance drivers' cars.
problem: A deactivation or algorithmic pay cut can remove 30-100% of a driver's income overnight with no unemployment insurance, while record auto delinquencies (brief) mean many drivers carry stressed car loans. Individual income insurance has historically failed on moral hazard and adverse selection.
solution: A membership cover paying 2-4 weeks of trailing average earnings on (a) a verified platform deactivation, or (b) a regional earnings-per-hour index falling more than 25% against baseline, computed from pooled, driver-consented earnings data. Structure it through a fronting carrier or discretionary mutual, and offer credit unions a car-payment protection version.
why_now: Record auto delinquencies, growing algorithmic management of pay, driver data cooperatives and earnings-tracking apps that already pool consented data, and instant payout rails.
revenue_model: $10-$20 per month premium, credit-union-paid group premium bundled with car loans, and anonymized index data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Moral hazard is the classic reason income insurance fails, but a platform-controlled event (deactivation) and a pooled regional index are not something the worker can game. The data cooperatives already exist and are the missing underwriting input.
first_30_days: Partner with one driver co-op or large forum for a 300-member paid pilot with a capped reserve. Collect earnings-data consents, back-test the index triggers on historical data, and have a fronting partner review the structure.

title: Paid Caregiver Demonstration-Data Cooperative
one_liner: Home-care aides and family caregivers wear head cameras during non-intimate care tasks and earn revenue share from licensing that data to robot-foundation-model companies.
customer: Robotics labs and humanoid makers buying home-task demonstration data (Figure, 1X, Skild, Physical Intelligence, Generalist-class buyers), at $60-150 per usable hour. Home-care agencies are the distribution partner.
problem: Humanoid progress is bottlenecked on physical-world data. Data vendors already pay people to film themselves making coffee (XDOF about $50M annualized, Mecka projecting $100M ARR). Nobody has data on the hardest, highest-value home tasks: walker and transfer assistance, modified-diet meal prep, laundry and tidying around frail people. Meanwhile aides earn under $35k and agencies see 77-80% turnover.
solution: Give each aide a $150 camera kit and an on-device consent and blurring pipeline. Capture only task categories that avoid intimate care, with care-recipient or proxy consent per home. Pay a per-hour data premium on top of wages, which agencies use as a retention bonus, and sell curated, labeled datasets.
why_now: Robot data-as-a-service went from nothing to unicorn valuations in months (Sep 2026). Immigration crackdowns are draining the care workforce, so agencies are desperate for retention tools that do not raise Medicaid-capped rates.
revenue_model: License datasets at $60-150 per hour. Pay workers 30-40%, agency 10% and keep the remainder. Add curation and labeling fees.
non_obvious_insight: Robots cannot yet enter the homes that hold the training data they most need, but the lowest-paid workforce in America is already inside them. Data pay solves agencies' turnover problem at no cost to a squeezed Medicaid budget.
first_30_days: Sign one home-care agency and 20 aides for a pilot. Write a consent and privacy protocol with an elder-law attorney. Pre-sell a 500-hour dataset to one robotics lab using a sample of kitchen and laundry tasks.

title: Parametric Outage Cover for Satellite Internet Users
one_liner: A $60 probe network and parametric policy that pays cash when a satellite-dependent operation loses connectivity.
customer: Mines, farms, offshore and maritime fleets, remote clinics and construction firms whose operations run on a single LEO link.
problem: Insiders treat Starlink as a utility. Operator SLAs give small credits, while the customer's loss is stopped production, idle crews or a stalled remote-operations center. Insurers avoid the risk because they have no independent measurement.
solution: Ship a probe that actively tests the customer's link and cross-checks against a global mesh of other probes. That produces tamper-resistant uptime evidence. Sell a parametric policy that pays a fixed amount per hour beyond a threshold, underwritten by an MGA and reinsurers. Add failover advice and an independent uptime scorecard for SLA negotiation.
why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, and enterprise, maritime and rural operations now depend on it. A widely reported global outage in July 2025 (prior knowledge) showed correlated failure is real. Amazon and others are launching alternatives to fail over to.
revenue_model: Probe subscription $30-100 per month per site. Premium about 4-8% of annual connectivity spend once the policy launches. Data licensing to reinsurers.
non_obvious_insight: Correlated single-vendor outages are actually easy to model, and the true blocker was measurement, not appetite. A cheap independent probe network converts an 'uninsurable' risk into a priced one.
first_30_days: Build the probe on a Raspberry Pi and deploy on 50 friendly terminals from RV, farm and maritime communities. Publish an uptime dashboard. Approach two MGAs about a pilot policy and sell probe subscriptions to three fleets.

title: Batteries That Pay Off Utility Arrears
one_liner: Install free home batteries in households behind on bills and let capacity payments retire the debt, which is cheaper for the utility than writing it off.
customer: Utilities, co-ops and munis in high-capacity-price regions (PJM first) that run arrears and shutoff programs. State PUCs and community action agencies co-sponsor. The utility pays from bad-debt and program budgets.
problem: 13.4M households were disconnected in 2024 and about 1 in 6 are behind on bills. Rates rose 7.3% in a year and this is a midterm issue. At the $325/MW-day cap, each kW of dispatchable capacity is worth about $118 a year, so a 5 kW home battery is worth roughly $590 a year gross, before accreditation haircuts and the aggregator's share.
solution: A no-cost 10 kWh 'bill-relief battery' for arrears households, enrolled in a utility or aggregator capacity program. Capacity and energy revenue is credited against the arrears balance for 5-7 years, after which the customer keeps it or the utility retains it. The company handles installation, financing and dispatch. The utility gets less bad debt and fewer politically toxic shutoffs.
why_now: Capacity prices hit the cap, packs cost about $70/kWh, dispatch at scale is proven, and utilities are under political pressure on affordability with few tools.
revenue_model: Per-install fee, a share of capacity revenue while the arrears are being retired, utility program payments, and project finance spread.
non_obvious_insight: At this capacity price, a battery earns more than it costs to give one away. Utility bad debt is a hidden capex budget that has never been spent on assets.
first_30_days: Get one utility's arrears distribution and model unit economics under current capacity prices. Pitch five community action agencies and three co-ops or munis on a 50-home pilot funded by weatherization-adjacent money. Line up a philanthropic first-loss guarantee.

title: Tenant Childcare Consortium Powered by 45F Credits
one_liner: Turn a vacant floor in a multi-tenant office or medical office building into a shared licensed childcare center whose seats are bought by 10-40 small tenant employers, each claiming the expanded 45F credit through a landlord-led consortium.
customer: Landlords of class-B office and medical office buildings (setup and management fee), small employers in those buildings (compliance fee and seat purchases), and a specialist childcare operator.
problem: Office vacancy is 17.8% nationally and lenders face $39B of office debt maturing in 12 months, so landlords need sticky tenants. Small employers cannot justify their own center. From 2026 the 45F credit is 40% (50% for small businesses) of qualified childcare spending, capped at $500K ($600K), and the law now lets an intermediary contract with childcare facilities for several employers. Almost no one has built the intermediary. Hospitals, clinics and professional-services firms in medical office buildings have severe shift-worker childcare gaps.
solution: The landlord donates or discounts a vacant suite (ideally lower floors) and a TI allowance. A licensed operator runs the center. The platform acts as the intermediary entity: it signs seat contracts with 10-40 tenants, documents each employer's qualified expenditure for the credit (Form 8882), pools and re-allocates unused seats among tenants, and helps employees route the DCFSA. A third-party operator whose principal business is childcare also sidesteps the 30%-employee-enrollment test that trips up in-house employer centers (to be confirmed with tax counsel).
why_now: The OBBBA expansion took effect for tax years beginning after Dec 31, 2025, so employers are setting 2026 and 2027 budgets now, and the year-end rush to lock 2026 credits is a natural sales moment. Landlords are under maturity-wall pressure and compete on amenities.
revenue_model: Landlord setup fee plus an NOI share of the operating margin (about 10%), a per-employer compliance fee (3-5% of credit value), and operator management fees.
non_obvious_insight: The credit turns a landlord amenity into a purchasing cooperative: alone a 40-person tenant cannot justify a center, but 20 together can, and the credit is richest for exactly the small businesses that fill class-B buildings. A child's seat is also far stickier than free rent as a lease-renewal driver, because losing the lease means losing the seat.
first_30_days: Approach five owners of medical office buildings and suburban office parks with 20%+ vacancy in a high-cost childcare metro. Survey tenants with a two-question form to size seat demand. Line up an operator and a tax counsel opinion memo. Aim to sign 8-10 employer seat contracts before December 2026 so they capture credits for this tax year.

title: Deadline-Proof AI Overflow and PII Shield for CPA Firms
one_liner: A browser extension that strips client SSNs, EINs and bank numbers before any AI tool sees them, and routes work to a compliant pay-as-you-go model when the firm's licensed AI hits its usage cap in the middle of a deadline.
customer: Accounting, tax and bookkeeping firms with 3 to 30 people, plus the MSPs that run their IT. All of them have written-security-program duties under the FTC Safeguards Rule.
problem: In 2026 vendors are moving to usage-based AI billing (Microsoft now uses Copilot Credits with administrator spending limits). When a firm's tool hits its cap mid-deadline, staff face three options: work stops, costs climb, or they improvise with personal consumer accounts. Uploading client statements and spreadsheets to unvetted tools breaks the Safeguards Rule's service-provider oversight requirement. Firms have no visibility into what left the building.
solution: A lightweight extension and gateway. First, it detects client PII (SSNs, EINs, account and routing numbers, dates of birth) in prompts and uploads and swaps in reversible tokens, with the mapping kept locally on the user's device. Second, it meters each seat's usage against the firm's licensed tools and, at 80% of a cap, offers an approved overflow route to a zero-retention model API billed at wholesale token cost plus a margin. Third, it writes an audit log that maps directly onto the firm's written information security program: who used what, which data classes were blocked, and which vendors were approved. Pre-purchased burst capacity is sold before each crunch (Oct 15 extension deadline, Mar 15, Apr 15).
why_now: The relevant CPA Practice Advisor article is dated Sept 28, 2026 (today). The Oct 15 extension deadline is 17 days away. Usage-based AI billing became normal this year. Firms are cutting headcount but software costs don't fall with it, so overflow spend competes with shrinking budgets.
revenue_model: $19 per seat per month for the shield and audit log, plus metered overflow at token cost +30%. Burst-capacity packs of $99 to $499 per season. MSPs and state CPA society partnerships get a channel margin of about 20%.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not the AI model, it is the capacity cliff at the worst possible moment, which pushes careful staff into shadow tools. CPA Practice Advisor states: 'When a firm's AI tool hits its usage cap mid-deadline, staff often turn to free consumer tools', cites the FTC Safeguards Rule requirement for a written information security program and oversight of service providers, and quotes IBM's finding that high shadow-AI usage adds about $670,000 to breach costs, with 63% of breached organizations having no AI governance policy (https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2026/09/28/token-limits-are-creating-a-shadow-ai-problem-for-accounting-firms/190633/). A companion piece shows why buying more seats isn't the answer: software costs stay flat when headcount falls, with contracts fixed until the notice deadline (https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2026/09/03/why-client-software-costs-dont-fall-when-headcount-does-and-what-advisors-should-review/189557/).
first_30_days: Week 1: build the redaction extension for Chrome/Edge with regex plus a small detector, and a simple metering dashboard. Pitch it in accounting communities and state CPA society newsletters as a 'get through Oct 15' tool. Weeks 2 to 3: onboard 10 firms free for the extension season in exchange for testimonials and audit-log feedback. Week 4: convert to $19 per seat and sell burst packs ahead of the next crunch; approach two MSPs that serve CPA firms. Target: 8 paying firms and 1 MSP partner.

title: Paid Shelter-Dog Field Trips, Fees Per Adoption
one_liner: Professional walkers take the longest-stay shelter dogs on 3-hour public field trips with photos and behavior reports, and shelters pay a small trip fee plus a success fee for each adoption.
customer: Municipal and county shelters and large humane societies (paying for outcomes), with pet-food brands, pet insurers, and community foundations as sponsors.
problem: Big adult dogs, especially bully-breed types, sit in kennels for months. Kennel stress makes them look their worst: barking, spinning, lunging. Adopters decide in about 30 seconds. Volunteers do field trips but are untrained for the hard dogs, unreliable, and unscalable. Every extra day in the kennel costs the shelter real money and raises the odds of a bad outcome.
solution: A walker collects the dog for a 3-hour outing in an 'Adopt Me' vest along a cafe, park, and errand route. They shoot 10 standardized photos and video, and file a behavior report (leash manners, other dogs, cats, car ride, house-training, energy). That content goes onto the shelter's listing and a hyperlocal 'Dog of the Week' list pushed through the walker's client network. Adopted dogs get a paid 7-day decompression check-in that also reduces returns. Everything is tracked against matched dogs to prove the effect on length of stay.
why_now: Shelters have been running over capacity for the past few years, with intake outpacing adoption and large dogs backing up, and budgets are tight. Housing and landlord pet restrictions keep driving relinquishments. Funders and municipalities increasingly want outcome-based spending, and walkers now have the cheap phone video and social distribution to make a dog look like a dog and not like a kennel number. I could not re-verify current national shelter statistics in this session, so quote local data in the pitch.
revenue_model: About $35 to $50 per field trip paid by the shelter or a sponsor, plus a $150 to $300 success fee per adoption within 30 days. Benchmark the success fee against the shelter's own cost per kennel day. Optional sponsored 'field trip' slots from pet brands and insurers, and grant funding to seed the first shelter.
non_obvious_insight: A dog is evaluated in the worst possible environment, and the fix is not better marketing, it is moving the evaluation out of the kennel. Professional walkers have exactly what volunteers lack: leash skill with hard dogs, idle midday capacity, and a trusted network of 50 to 100 households that will actually meet a dog because the walker they trust is holding the leash.
first_30_days: Offer the shelter's volunteer or foster coordinator a free pilot on the 10 longest-stay dogs, with two or three of your own walkers. Track days-to-adoption against similar dogs not taken out. After 30 days, hand the director a one-page results sheet and ask for a paid pilot, or apply for a local pet-industry or community foundation grant to fund the first 100 trips.

title: Pay-Per-Decibel Neighbor Trust for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent trust that owns a sensor mesh around a data center and automatically pays nearby households every time the hum exceeds agreed limits, turning 'trust us' into a self-executing contract.
customer: Data center developers and hyperscaler community-affairs teams, their land-use counsel, and counties negotiating community benefit agreements. Pre-application projects facing a rezoning fight are the entry point.
problem: Local opposition blocked or delayed roughly $130B of US data center projects in 2026, and opposition groups more than doubled to 833 by March. Developers' flat checks get called bribes: a $10,000-per-household offer to 4,500 households was rejected by residents in September. Noise promises are unenforceable, and dBA ordinances miss the low-frequency hum residents complain about. Counties lack staff to monitor compliance.
solution: A neighbor trust, funded by a developer bond, with three parts. (1) Trust-owned acoustic, low-frequency and vibration sensors, publicly viewable in real time. (2) A pre-agreed parametric schedule: any household within the radius gets an automatic payment for each night the level exceeds the threshold, so the payout works like a warranty on quiet. (3) Escalation funding for window and HVAC retrofits if exceedances persist. The trust also reports compliance to the county, giving regulators enforcement without new staff.
why_now: Opposition is peaking (about 120 projects stalled in H1 2026, more than 300 state bills, moratoria such as New York's), and developers are now experimenting with direct household payments and getting burned on credibility. Developers now need a neutral administrator, and no obvious specialist exists.
revenue_model: Developer pays $150k to $500k setup per campus, plus 8% to 12% of the annual fund as administration, plus sensor-as-a-service fees. Add county compliance-monitoring contracts. A single multi-billion-dollar campus can absorb this as a rounding error against months of delay.
non_obvious_insight: Neighbors rarely reject data centers over money. They reject unmeasured, unpriced harm. Making the harm measured and self-paying changes the negotiation and gives the developer a real financial reason to buy quieter chillers and dampers. The low-frequency, night-time signature is what the trust measures, and ordinances miss it.
first_30_days: List the next five county hearings on data center rezoning from local news and Data Center Watch. Hire a freelance acoustic engineer and build a $2k-per-node sensor kit from off-the-shelf parts. Offer a free 60-day neutral baseline noise map to one pending project, in front of both the developer and the opposition group. Convert that goodwill into a paid pre-application baseline of $50k to $100k and an MOU for the trust structure.

title: Distributor Credit Radar for Failing Restaurants
one_liner: A weekly early-warning score on each restaurant account, built from public signals and distributors' own order and payment data, so food distributors can tighten terms before the customer goes dark.
customer: Independent foodservice distributors (produce, protein, dairy, beverage, paper) with $20-500M in revenue that sell on net-14 and net-30 terms to restaurants. The buyer is the credit manager, controller or owner.
problem: Restaurants are high-turnover, thinly capitalized credit risks, and distributors are unsecured creditors who see the problem last. Generic credit bureaus are weak on restaurants. When consumer spending is squeezed and rates are higher, bad debt climbs and distributors respond with blunt tools (COD for everyone) that lose good accounts.
solution: A risk score per account, refreshed weekly, combining health-inspection trends, permit and liquor-license status, lien and judgment filings, review and hours changes, delivery-platform activity, foot traffic, and the distributor's own signals (order-size decline, days-to-pay drift). Alerts recommend cutting limits, switching to COD or accelerating collection. A consortium data pool of anonymized payment experience improves the score for every member. A bad-debt shield insurance product can follow.
why_now: Squeezed lower-income consumers, higher borrowing costs and the energy-cost shock raise restaurant failures. Public and alternative data on restaurants is now cheap to assemble, and distributors are digitizing accounts receivable and order data.
revenue_model: $600-2,500 per month per distributor by account count, plus consortium data access and later an insurance referral share.
non_obvious_insight: Restaurants fail visibly weeks or months before they stop paying. The best predictor is the distributor's own order-size decline, which they are not analyzing, and the consortium effect (shared payment behavior) becomes a data moat no single distributor can build.
first_30_days: Get three regional distributors to share two years of anonymized accounts-receivable history and back-test whether public signals warn 8-12 weeks before write-offs. Sell a paid pilot at $1,500 per month. Each avoided $20k write-off pays for the subscription for a year.

title: Exoskeletons That Delay Tradesperson Retirement
one_liner: Lease passive and powered exoskeletons with fitting, coaching and outcome-based pricing to shops and insurers, targeting 55+ tradespeople whose retirement drives the labor gap.
customer: Workers' comp carriers and PEOs, contractor associations, and 10-100 employee roofing, plumbing, HVAC, framing and drywall shops with aging crews.
problem: ABC says most of the 349K 2026 shortfall is retirements, and older tradespeople leave over knees, backs and shoulders. Replacement hiring is impossible in a market where trade-school enrollment hype is called a demographic mirage. Strain injuries also drive comp claims.
solution: Vetted kits (passive shoulder and back supports, emerging powered hip and knee assists), professional fitting, a task playbook for overhead, attic, roofing and crawlspace work, and usage and injury-risk telemetry. Monthly lease with a guarantee tied to comp premium reduction or absence rates, piloted with carriers first.
why_now: Powered assist suits have fallen from tens of thousands of dollars to low thousands per unit. Comp carriers face margin pressure and want proven loss-control tools. The retirement wave now dominates the labor gap, and hiring cannot fill it.
revenue_model: $150-300 per worker per month lease, a carrier program fee, and outcome-based rebates.
non_obvious_insight: This is a retention and insurance business, not a robotics business: the cheapest new journeyman is the 62-year-old who did not retire. The buyer with the incentive and the loss data is the comp carrier, not the worker or the owner.
first_30_days: Approach two regional comp carriers or PEOs with a 60-day pilot. Sign three shops (10 workers total) and measure discomfort, absences and adoption. Secure wholesale terms with one exoskeleton supplier and one trade association endorsement.

title: Civil-Document Runners for Immigrant Families
one_liner: A vetted in-country network that retrieves, verifies and delivers birth, marriage, police and court records for consular and NVC cases, with chain-of-custody proof and no forged shortcuts.
customer: Immigration law firms and family-based petitioners (largely South Asian, Filipino, West African and Latin American communities) who pay $150-450 per document, plus rush fees and bundled certified translation and apostille.
problem: Applicants wait on USCIS, but the delays that lawyers dread most sit at the National Visa Center and consulate: 'documentarily qualified' rejections, requests for secondary evidence, and 221(g) refusals for a missing or irregular civil document. Every country issues records differently, and the State Department's reciprocity schedule is only a starting point. Families hire fixers or relatives, sometimes receive forged or improperly obtained records, and then face a permanent fraud bar (INA 212(a)(6)(C)). Lawyers keep private lists of trusted runners abroad. They cannot scale and are not available to families without counsel.
solution: A managed marketplace of vetted local partners (lawyers, licensed document agents, registry liaisons) in 8-10 high-volume corridors (India, Philippines, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nigeria, Vietnam, El Salvador, Haiti). Each order starts with a pre-check against the consulate's actual document list, then a tracked retrieval from the issuing office with receipt and photo proof, an 'authenticity file' documenting exactly how the record was obtained, and delivery bundled with certified translation, apostille where applicable, and secondary-evidence packets when a record truly doesn't exist. Use online registries (India DigiLocker, Philippines PSA, Mexico's online actas) wherever possible so that most orders need little or no physical runner.
why_now: Consular processing has become slower and more discretionary, with more document-authenticity scrutiny, more public-charge-related evidence demands, and periodic pauses or holds by nationality. Errors that used to cost weeks now cost months. Many civil registries have digitized since 2020, so remote retrieval is now feasible for a meaningful share of documents, which makes a thin-margin logistics business viable for a small team.
revenue_model: Per-document fee ($150-450 depending on country and rush), roughly 40-50% gross margin after local partner costs, plus bundled translation and apostille, and a subscription tier for firms that order 20 or more documents a month.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody thinks of immigration as a logistics problem, so VCs fund form software while the real bottleneck is a birth certificate in a district registry that doesn't respond to email. The valuable asset is not software but a scorecard of which local partners and registry offices actually deliver on time and produce documents consulates accept. Reliability data by country and office can be built only by handling volume, and that is a moat lawyers already acknowledge privately.
first_30_days: Pick three corridors (Philippines, Mexico, India) where much of the retrieval can be done through official online portals plus one local partner. Sign 2 partners per corridor and pilot with 5 family-immigration firms at a flat price per document. Handle every order by hand, log time-to-delivery and rejection rates by office, and publish a country-by-country reliability guide to attract the next firms.

title: Human Trust-Anchor Service for Driverless Freight Hubs
one_liner: A neutral crew and signature service at autonomous-truck terminals that replaces the driver's role as freight's witness: pre-trip inspection, condition-of-freight capture, signed digital BOL and inspector liaison, priced per handoff.
customer: Autonomous trucking carriers, the shippers, 3PLs and brokers tendering freight to them, and cargo insurers. The first buyer is a claims-sensitive shipper or a broker like Werner's CIO who says 'we have a gap'.
problem: The driver signs the BOL, counts pieces, notes damage, checks the seal and talks to the inspector. Driverless trucks remove that witness. The CVSA enhanced-inspection clearance lasts 24 hours and requires a trained inspector. PrePass/Kodiak bypass covers 581 sites but is live only in Texas and Louisiana. Paper BOLs delay cash about 60 days and cause six-figure invoice disputes. Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff. Insurers price AV trucks above human ones purely on the unknown.
solution: A per-departure witness desk at transfer hubs and terminals, staffed by trained ex-drivers and ex-inspectors with capture tools. It runs the pre-trip enhanced-inspection checklist and logs the 24-hour clearance. It captures condition of freight (piece count, seal number, photos, weight, temperature, damage detection) and issues a neutral third-party-signed eBOL that shipper, carrier and insurer accept. It also acts as the roadside and first-responder liaison, and packages claims evidence.
why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and targets 30,000 by 2030. Gatik reports 85k driverless orders. California's driverless-truck rules took effect Apr 28, 2026 and the Teamsters sued on Aug 5. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on Jul 8, 2026. Insurers expect AV truck pricing to fall 15-25% a year, so evidence of loads and conditions moves pricing.
revenue_model: $35-$90 per handoff or departure, well under the current human transfer cost. $4k-$8k/mo per hub as a base fee. Insurer-paid discounts and data license. Claims-evidence packages at $150-$400 per incident.
non_obvious_insight: Driverless trucking is sold as removing labor, but what it actually removes is a witness, and freight claims, inspections and insurance pricing all ran on that witness. Whoever re-supplies trusted witness capacity at transfer hubs becomes a required, neutral node. Because the same crew and signature service serve every AV carrier, no competing carrier will build it.
first_30_days: Pick one Texas corridor and one terminal. Recruit 2-3 ex-inspectors or ex-drivers. Offer a shipper's claims team or a broker a free pilot on 20 AV loads, then $60 per handoff. Sign a cargo insurer as design partner to co-develop the claims-evidence package.

title: Pay the Grandmother: Relative-Care Subsidy Enrollment
one_liner: A multilingual concierge plus verified-attendance software that turns unpaid grandparents and relatives into subsidy-paid, health-and-safety-cleared caregivers, billed per enrollment to states and referral agencies.
customer: State child-care subsidy (CCDF) lead agencies, county subsidy offices and child care resource and referral (CCR&R) agencies. Secondary: workforce boards and Head Start grantees.
problem: Deserts are measured in licensed slots (3+ kids per slot), but most parents actually cobble together relative care that the maps never count. Many states can already pay license-exempt relatives through subsidy. Families don't enroll because of fingerprinting, training, provider agreements and slow payment. States are also wary of fraud (federal subsidy-fraud scrutiny in winter 2025-26, from memory, not verified). So the 'supply' looks empty while grandmothers work for free.
solution: A guided onboarding flow in the caregiver's language covers document collection, fingerprint appointment booking, CPR and safe-sleep micro-training, and e-signed provider agreements. Attendance is logged by phone tap-in with geo-stamp and parent co-sign, which gives the state verified attendance. Payment goes out by direct deposit or prepaid card within days. A state dashboard shows 'real supply unlocked' by county.
why_now: Childcare costs hit about $13,128 a year (up 29% since 2020) while licensed supply barely grows (centers +1.5%, homes +4.3% in 2024). The 2024 federal CCDF rule (7% copay cap, enrollment-based prospective payment) is being implemented by states in 2025-26 (from memory). Universal-care promises (NYC per the brief) create demand for supply that needs no buildings. Fraud scrutiny makes verified attendance a selling point, not a cost.
revenue_model: Per completed enrollment fee ($150-400) plus a per-active-caregiver monthly fee ($3-8), paid by the agency under a pilot contract. Pilots run $30-60k per CCR&R or county.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in childcare deserts is not buildings or workers. It is unpaid supply that already exists, blocked by paperwork and by states' fear of fraud. The winner sells verified attendance as much as enrollment.
first_30_days: Pick two states with permissive relative-care rules. Map every enrollment step and drop-off point. Offer one CCR&R a free 25-family concierge pilot run over WhatsApp and phone, with Twilio and a no-code form behind it. Recruit through Spanish-, Somali- and Hmong-speaking community groups. Get a letter of intent from one county for a paid per-enrollment fee.
